steps.body:
You now have five questions, and in this order they catch almost everything:

1. **How was the data made?** (design → ceiling)
2. **Who was left out?** (bias — the margin cannot see it)
3. **How much wobble?** (margin of error)
4. **Is the effect bigger than the wobble?** (significance)
5. **Is it big enough to matter?** (effect size)

explanationVariants: The sample is enormous but self-selected — app users who chose to answer. Question 2 fails, and the tiny margin in question 3 is measuring the wrong thing.
A precise number from a broken frame is the most dangerous object in statistics.

widget.prompt: "In a survey of 300,000 of our app's users, 78% ± 0.2% say the app improved their focus." Which question does this claim fail first?

options.label: Who was left out — only app users who chose to respond are in it.
options.feedback: Right, and it fails at question 2, which means the ±0.2% is precision about a group nobody asked about.

options.label: How much wobble — the sample is too small.
options.feedback: 300,000 makes the wobble tiny. That is precisely why the bias is so dangerous here.

options.label: Is the effect big enough — 78% is not much.
options.feedback: 78% would be a large number if it meant anything. The problem arrives earlier, at who was asked.

options.label: It fails nothing — the sample is huge.
options.feedback: Size is not representativeness. Every respondent chose both to use the app and to answer the survey.

steps.body: Run the five questions on a real-shaped claim.

widget.prompt: "New drug cuts recovery time by 12 hours (p = 0.03, 40 patients)."

panels.title: Questions 1 and 2
panels.body: Were patients randomly assigned? If yes, a causal claim is available for patients like these. If they chose the drug, the claim collapses to association immediately.

panels.title: Questions 3 and 4
panels.body: Forty patients is a small study, so the wobble is large. p = 0.03 clears the conventional bar, but only just — and one small study clearing 0.05 is exactly what a fluke looks like.

panels.title: Question 5
panels.body: Twelve hours off a recovery: is that worth the drug's cost and side effects? Statistics has now done its whole job. This last question is a judgement, and it is yours.

widget.continueFeedback: Keep going — the last question is not a statistical one.
widget.successFeedback: The tools tell you whether the effect is real and how big it is. Whether it is worth having is a decision, and the numbers never make it for you.

explanationVariants: A randomised trial licenses cause; the p-value clears the bar; but a 0.4-point gain on a 100-point test fails question 5.
Real and trivial. The design is clean and the finding is still not worth buying.

widget.prompt: "A randomised trial of 80,000 students found the tool raised scores by 0.4 points (p < 0.001)." Which question does it fail?

options.label: Question 5 — the effect is real but far too small to matter.
options.feedback: Right. The design is impeccable and the evidence is strong. The effect is simply not worth having.

options.label: Question 1 — the design cannot support a causal claim.
options.feedback: It was randomised, so cause is licensed. The design is the one thing this study got right.

options.label: Question 4 — the effect is not bigger than the wobble.
options.feedback: With 80,000 students the wobble is tiny, which is exactly why 0.4 points cleared it. It passes question 4 and fails the next one.

options.label: It fails nothing — p < 0.001 settles it.
options.feedback: p < 0.001 settles question 4 and nothing else. It has no opinion on whether 0.4 points is worth a purchase order.

steps.body:
Two habits worth keeping for life:

**Ask what was randomised** before you read anything else. It is one question and it settles what the claim may say.

**Read the band, not the number.** Every estimate is a range, every gap has its own wobble, and every "significant" finding still owes you an effect size.

explanationVariants: Twelve patients cannot rule out chance: a p-value of 0.30 says data like this arise easily when nothing is happening.
A promising effect size with no evidence behind it is a reason to run a bigger study, not to prescribe anything.

widget.prompt: Sort each finding: act on it, or wait?

items.label: Randomised, n = 900, +14 points, p = 0.001
items.feedback: Clean design, large effect, strong evidence. All five questions pass.

items.label: Randomised, n = 12, +14 points, p = 0.30
items.feedback: The effect looks big, but twelve patients cannot rule out luck. Run a bigger trial before acting.

items.label: Observational, n = 200,000, +14 points, p < 0.001
items.feedback: Precise and probably real — but nothing was assigned, so a lurking variable could be producing the whole gap.

items.label: Randomised, n = 5,000, +0.2 points, p = 0.004
items.feedback: Real and trivial. The study is sound; the effect is not worth the trouble.

widget.missFeedback: Only a randomised design, a large enough effect, and evidence against chance together justify acting.
widget.successFeedback: One finding passes all five questions. The other three fail a different one each — design, evidence, and size.

hints: Start with question 1: what was randomised? Nothing — the cities chose their own policies.
So no causal claim is available, whatever the p-value says. Note the huge sample makes the association precise, not causal.
Then check the effect size and ask whether a 2% difference in a self-selected set of cities could plausibly come from the kind of city that adopts such a policy.
explanationVariants: Cities chose their own policies, so this is observational: the 2% gap is an association, and cities that adopt such policies likely differ in many other ways.
The 500,000 residents make the estimate precise. Precision about an association is still an association, and 2% is a small effect besides.

widget.prompt: "Cities with the new recycling policy have 2% less landfill waste (500,000 residents surveyed, p < 0.001). Every city should adopt it." What is the strongest objection?

options.label: The cities chose their own policies, so this is observational — the kind of city that adopts it may already recycle more.
options.feedback: Right, and this is question 1. No amount of data or significance can promote an association to a cause.

options.label: p < 0.001 is suspiciously small.
options.feedback: With half a million residents, a small p-value is exactly what you would expect even from a trivial association. It is not suspicious, just uninformative about cause.

options.label: The sample is too small to support a policy change.
options.feedback: 500,000 residents is a very large sample. The break is in the design, not the size.

options.label: 2% is impossible to measure accurately.
options.feedback: It is perfectly measurable, and the margin here is tiny. The problem is what the 2% is allowed to mean.

takeaways: Design first (what was randomised?), then who was left out, then the wobble, then whether the effect clears it, then whether it matters.
Bias is invisible to the margin of error, and significance is invisible to the question of size.
The numbers tell you what is real and how big. Whether it is worth doing is a judgement — and it stays yours.
steps.teaser: You have finished the inference strand: from how data is made to what a claim may honestly say.

concept.body: Take the questions in order and stop at the first failure. A claim that fails question 1 cannot be rescued by a beautiful p-value at question 4 — the later answers are only meaningful once the earlier ones pass.

explanationVariants: Nothing was randomly assigned, so the claim fails at question 1 and the rest of the audit cannot save it.
Design failures are fatal; later strengths cannot compensate for them.

widget.prompt: An observational study with a perfect sample, a tiny margin, p < 0.001 and a huge effect claims a CAUSE. Where does it fail?

options.label: Question 1 — nothing was randomly assigned, so no causal claim is available.
options.feedback: Right. Everything downstream is excellent and none of it can promote an association to a cause.

options.label: Question 3 — the margin must be wrong.
options.feedback: The margin is fine. The problem is that the design never licensed the word 'cause' in the first place.
